item.title: India-UK investment treaty talks stall amid differences, pact unlikely soon
item.description: A bilateral investment treaty protects companies' investments in each other's countries and provides a way to resolve disputes with governments ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India does not plan to aggressively pursue a bilateral investment treaty with Britain in the near term, as differences over taxation and access to international arbitration continue to stall negotiations, two senior government officials said.India's reluctance comes as it seeks to negotiate investment treaties alongside trade agreements with major partners, including the European Union and Canada, to provide reciprocal protection to investors and boost confidence in cross-border investments.A bilateral investment treaty protects companies' investments in each other's countries and provides a way to resolve disputes with governments.British companies, including Vodafone and Cairn, have won international arbitration cases against India over retrospective tax claims and the cancellation of contracts worth billions of dollars.About a decade ago, India allowed treaties with over 50 countries to lapse and then designed a law that limits the protection offered to investors. That law is also under review.The first source, who is involved in the discussions and not authorised to speak to the media, said the talks had lost momentum and a pact was unlikely in the near term.New Delhi wants to preserve its sovereign right to set tax and regulatory policy, while Britain wants stronger investor protections, including easier access to international arbitration, the source said.The differences kept the treaty from being concluded alongside the countries' free trade agreement, which took effect on July 15, they said.Emails sent to India's trade and finance ministries seeking comment did not receive a response. The UK's finance ministry also did not respond to a request for comment.The UK was India's ninth-largest source of foreign direct investment equity inflows in 2025/26, investing more than $1 billion, according to government data.Officials from both countries are expected to meet in early December for the UK-India Economic and Financial Dialogue, a ministerial-level forum covering macroeconomic policy, financial regulation, taxation and climate finance, the second source said. However, the investment treaty will not be discussed there, they added.The dialogue, co-chaired by India's finance minister and Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, will be the first under UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. The two sides last held it in April 2025, under the previous British government.Separately, tensions have risen recently over India's decision to impose a 162.5% import duty on bulk Scotch whisky, which has prompted a dispute with liquor firms including Pernod Ricard and Diageo.INDIA REVIEWS INVESTMENT TREATY FRAMEWORKIndia's stance reflects a broader effort to limit the exposure of domestic policy decisions to international legal challenges following high-profile arbitration disputes.In 2015, New Delhi proposed a new treaty framework that excludes tax and prevents investors from seeking international arbitration before exhausting local remedies. It has since signed revised agreements with countries including the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, Israel, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.The 2015 model is now being reviewed again. India plans to retain the requirement that foreign investors exhaust local legal remedies before seeking international arbitration, though the mandatory five-year period could be shortened to two years, the second source said.Treaties signed with the UAE in 2024 and Israel in 2025, both now in force, allow investors to seek international arbitration after three years instead of five.The government is close to securing Cabinet approval for a revised model treaty that will serve as the basis for negotiations with individual countries, a senior official told reporters in September.India is currently negotiating free trade agreements with at least eight countries, alongside parallel investment treaty talks with many of them.

Sebi to ease KYC norms, centralise client details at registration agencies The revised norms, effective December 24, will simplify client onboarding by eliminating repeated submission of supplementary KYC details and enabling portability of records

Sebi has revised KYC norms to simplify investor onboarding, centralise supplementary client details at registration agencies and make verified records portable across market intermediaries. | Image: Bloomberg

Our Bureau 1 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 5:49 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Wednesday announced changes to simplify client onboarding, under which common supplementary know-your-customer (KYC) details will be centralised at KYC registration agencies (KRAs). Investors will not have to resubmit them to each intermediary. Intermediaries will be able to skip mobile number verification if the KRA database already shows the number as verified and Aadhaar-seeded. Records whose attributes, including either the current or permanent address, are verified against official databases will be tagged "validated" and will be portable across intermediaries. Intermediaries will also have to inform KRAs of account closures within five working days. The changes will come into force on December 24, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Sharp November run-up dims mkt's risk-reward ratio; volatility likely: KIE

Sharp November run-up dims mkt's risk-reward ratio; volatility likely: KIE The Indian equity markets have surged 10 per cent so far in November as foreign investors returned to Dalal Street with full force, ploughing in a record ₹1.3 trillion in this month so far.

Image Credit: Bloomberg

Saloni Goel New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 25 2026 | 12:50 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The sharp rally in Indian equities in November has made the market's risk-reward proposition less favourable, even as domestic fundamentals remain supportive, according to Kotak Institutional Equities (KIE).    The Indian equity markets have surged 10 per cent so far in November as foreign investors returned to Dalal Street with full force, ploughing in a record ₹1.3 trillion in this month so far.    Therefore, even as KIE remains 'constructive' on the Indian stock market, it doesn't rule out highly volatility. "We expect increased volatility in the near term, linked to global investment sentiment," the brokerage said.   It noted that Indian market would have to contend with the sharper fall in other DM and EM markets in the past month, the sharp deterioration in global risk sentiment and/or possible resurgence of ‘AI trade’.

The brokerage said the reversal in global markets over the past one-and-a-half months could have been triggered by several concerns, including questions around chipmakers' earnings, the pace of AI adoption, the total addressable market for large language models, the sustainability of AI-related capital expenditure and stretched valuations.   CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates Also Read

While concerns around the pace of AI adoption and data centre investments could be weighing on global sentiment, KIE believes these developments are unlikely to have a meaningful direct impact on India. Any spill over to domestic equities would largely be through the sentiment perspective, and factors like earnings and oil will be bigger determinants.

"We expect market returns to be largely driven by crude prices in the near term, and earnings in the medium term. The sharp run-up in the market and stocks across ‘consumption’ sectors in the past week would suggest that the market is already factoring in lower crude oil prices and higher margins in FY2028," said the brokerage.   It added that both would play out on improved crude supply-demand balance in CY2027, increased crude oil supply from the West Asia and Iran’s weak economy amid low oil production forcing it to seek a peace deal but note tail risks from a re-escalation in the Iran-US war.

Meanwhile, the brokerage finds large-caps stocks still at reasonable valuations, but sees limited rerating potential following the sharp run-up seen in largecap names. Stocks across automobiles, banks, consumer staples and telecommunications have already witnessed a re-rating over the past two to three weeks, it said.   Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited.
